title: An all-seeing eye
caption: The interacting galaxies IC 2163 and NGC 2207, imaged by ALMA and the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)/M. Kaufman & the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two galaxies overlap in this composite image, and the one on the left, IC 2163, has taken on a shape like a human eye. Its companion on the right is NGC 2207. The picture blends Hubble Space Telescope images with observations from ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

The pair lies approximately 114 million light-years away, toward the constellation of Canis Major. The two brushed together, their spiral arms touching only at the outer edges, with IC 2163 passing behind NGC 2207. That glancing blow sent a tsunami of stars and gas rushing inwards through IC 2163's disc. The wave slowed sharply and piled up partway through the disc, creating bright ribbons of intense star formation and squeezed ridges of gas and dust that look like a pair of eyelids.
Glancing collisions of this kind are fairly common, but eye-shaped structures are rarely seen.

understand.summary: This is a composite of Hubble images from its Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, taken through filters from 336 to 814 nm, and ALMA millimeter-wavelength observations of carbon monoxide gas. The colors assigned to each dataset are not published.
understand.eye: ALMA's millimeter-wavelength data trace cold gas that is completely invisible to the eye, so this view combines two very different kinds of light.

explore: Their rarity is probably because they do not last long. Such ocular shapes tend to survive only several tens of millions of years, a blink in a galaxy's lifetime. ALMA is a partnership of ESO, the U.S. National Science Foundation and Japan's National Institutes of Natural Sciences, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile.
